title: 'This article first appeared in City & Country, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026
body: 'It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge ’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception.  “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.”  The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd.  Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation.  Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore.  The ambitious development has made international headlines over the years, some of them for the wrong reasons, especially since it has fallen short of market expectations in terms of progress, sales and occupancy rates. These challenges were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic and the well-documented financial restructuring of its parent company amid China’s broader real estate liquidity crisis.  “When China’s property market faced a systemic downturn, amplified by global supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and strict pandemic controls, Country Garden — once China’s top property developer — was caught in the crossfire, just like many other big players in the country. However, late last year, our parent group successfully executed onshore and offshore debt restructurings in China,” says Li, who is also the chief financial officer of Country Garden Malaysia.  Regardless of the situation faced by its parent company, he highlights that Country Garden Malaysia operates with complete operational and financial independence.  “Since Country Garden entered Malaysia as its first overseas destination back in 2010 and 2011, the local operation has relied on an independent management team. For the past three years, our cash flow has been generated entirely within the country, allowing us to remain self-sustaining in terms of liquidity and debt servicing,” he says, adding that all five of its projects in the Klang Valley and Johor are performing steadily.  According to Li, Country Garden Malaysia’s sales and cash collection was RM1.3 billion in 2023, more than RM1.1 billion in 2024, and RM1.3 billion in 2025.  “More crucially, we utilised our local cash flows to fully settle bank borrowings and capital market obligations worth about RM2 billion over the past three years, including a RM1 billion sukuk … As at earlier this year, the remaining outstanding amount [of the sukuk] was only RM150 million. We pre-repaid them as our cash flow was comfortable.”  With most of its debts cleared, local rating agency RAM upgraded Country Garden Malaysia’s outlook rating from negative to stable in March, reflecting its balance-sheet resilience despite global sector volatility.  That financial stability has been supported by developments on the legal front. Malaysian courts have recently upheld the validity of sales and purchase agreements in favour of the developer. Dismissing buyer suits seeking to void contracts for reasons such as media portrayals of the project as a “ghost town”, the courts established that market downturns and post-purchase regret do not constitute grounds for breach. The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base.  “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. We understand that we cannot make every single person happy, and it is normal to receive feedback or complaints. We respect the buyers’ legal rights,” Li says.  “But we also have our internal KPIs [key performance indicators] to meet. We are pleased to share that customer satisfaction consistently hits above 95% in our surveys and polls. Generally, the majority of our 20,000 residents are happy to live here, or they wouldn’t choose to continue staying. This is evidenced by our growing population.”  A city waking up  Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank.  “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.”  Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities.  “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.”  Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore.  There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families.  “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says.  Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024.  Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers.  However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework.  Strategic shift  Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state.  “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul.  The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ.  In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates.  In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone.  “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li.  “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.”  To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors.  “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says.  Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them.  “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains.  Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive.  According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physi­cal office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date.  “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds.  Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur.  Forest City 2.0  Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility.  “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.”  To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals.  “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says.  For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. Once approved, ferry routes will connect Forest City directly to Raffles Marina in Singapore and Batam in Indonesia.  “We are also asking the government for assistance to permit a direct highway connection linking straight to Tuas, and to integrate Forest City into upcoming regional rail routes like the RTS [Rapid Transit System], ART [Automated Rapid Transit] and transport corridors heading to Kulai and Senai,” he adds. “Moving people efficiently is crucial to unlocking the full value of the JS-SEZ but because these are country-to-country matters, we have to keep pushing and following up continuously.”  Simultaneously, the master developer is pivoting to boosting population density and creating high-value local jobs, away from traditional residential property sales, towards what the team calls “Forest City 2.0”.  “We are not launching any more residential projects in the near future, but focusing on clearing the inventory. We will advance commercial and industrial land development earlier than originally scheduled to inject immediate economic vibrancy,” Li says. “Our next focus is to bring in companies and industries to invest or establish their presence here.”  Acknowledging the importance of generating sufficient jobs to increase Forest City’s population, CGPV is actively trying to draw data centres, logistics players and manufacturers to its upcoming 418-acre industrial park.  “We need to create real economic dynamics. If you don’t generate jobs and economic substance, you cannot sustain a population,” Li stresses.  The response to this industrial shift has been positive. In the first half of this year alone, the developer logged over 300 company enquiries and secured a 40-acre industrial land deal with a manufacturer in Phase 1 of the industrial park, paving the way for ready-built factory developments in Phase 2 should market demand sustain.  In another strategic partnership, Country Garden recently signed a term sheet with Penang-based Oriental Holdings Bhd (KL: ORIENT) to develop a RM750 million healthcare hub in Forest City, anchored by a 500-bed hospital alongside comprehensive medical supply chain services.  “Internationally, we are actively introducing Forest City to big-name [multinational corporations]. It is not so much for their name, but the entire supply chain. We are looking to bring in ‘queen bee’ investors,” Li says. “We have been doing roadshows, especially in China, to introduce the JS-SEZ and Forest City SFZ. We went to Shenzhen and Suzhou, which have some of the most successful industrial parks in China.”  Apart from the industrial park, CGPV has also received enquiries from international investors interested in private island parcels.  “It is something that we are looking at. Instead of standard residential towers, we can custom-reclaim approved island plots, such as 1.5 to two acres, based entirely on an investor’s specific operational or residential requirements. It’s about being adaptive to what the current market actually demands,” he says.  Road to 2030 and beyond  Apart from Forest City, Country Garden Malaysia has four other major developments in Johor and the Klang Valley, executed largely through JVs.  “Out of our five projects in Malaysia, four are structured as JVs,” Li explains. “Only Danga Bay is 100% held by Country Garden Malaysia. We welcome JVs because local partners bring value to the table, though for master site design, we prefer to lead.”  In Johor Bahru, Country Garden Central Park has completed three phases comprising over 3,000 residential units that are nearly fully sold. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle.  In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period.  In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years.  With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade.  As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development.  “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward.  “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.”  He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone.  “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.”

'This article first appeared in City & Country, The Edge Malaysia Weekly on September 28, 2026 - October 4, 2026

'It was a scorching afternoon when Country Garden Pacificview Sdn Bhd (CGPV) executive director and chief of regional industrial business development Kevin Li and regional vice-president Syarul Izam Sarifudin arrived at The Edge ’s office in Petaling Jaya, Selangor. The pair had flown in from Johor Bahru to give an update on Forest City, a high-profile project in Johor that has dealt with some hot issues since its inception.  “What we achieved [since 2015] up to 2025 was merely concentrating more on our operational stability, resource integration and preparing for our next phase of growth,” says Syarul. “In the early years, we were primarily viewed as a residential real estate developer. But we are now embarking into a new sector — managing townships and driving actual economic nodes of financial and industrial development in southern Johor.”  The master developer of Forest City is a joint venture between China-headquartered developer Country Garden Holdings Co Ltd and Esplanade Danga 88 Sdn Bhd.  Operating as an independent local management unit under Country Garden Malaysia’s executive umbrella, CGPV is responsible for Forest City’s master plan development and management, industrial park development and Special Financial Zone (SFZ) operation.  Officially launched by the Malaysian government with duty-free island status in 2016, the 7,500-acre integrated development covers four reclaimed man-made islands over 5,000 acres and 2,500 acres on the mainland. Located in Iskandar Puteri, it sits along the Straits of Johor near the Malaysia-Singapore Second Link, just 2km across the water from Singapore.  The ambitious development has made international headlines over the years, some of them for the wrong reasons, especially since it has fallen short of market expectations in terms of progress, sales and occupancy rates. These challenges were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic and the well-documented financial restructuring of its parent company amid China’s broader real estate liquidity crisis.  “When China’s property market faced a systemic downturn, amplified by global supply chain disruptions, macroeconomic shifts and strict pandemic controls, Country Garden — once China’s top property developer — was caught in the crossfire, just like many other big players in the country. However, late last year, our parent group successfully executed onshore and offshore debt restructurings in China,” says Li, who is also the chief financial officer of Country Garden Malaysia.  Regardless of the situation faced by its parent company, he highlights that Country Garden Malaysia operates with complete operational and financial independence.  “Since Country Garden entered Malaysia as its first overseas destination back in 2010 and 2011, the local operation has relied on an independent management team. For the past three years, our cash flow has been generated entirely within the country, allowing us to remain self-sustaining in terms of liquidity and debt servicing,” he says, adding that all five of its projects in the Klang Valley and Johor are performing steadily.  According to Li, Country Garden Malaysia’s sales and cash collection was RM1.3 billion in 2023, more than RM1.1 billion in 2024, and RM1.3 billion in 2025.  “More crucially, we utilised our local cash flows to fully settle bank borrowings and capital market obligations worth about RM2 billion over the past three years, including a RM1 billion sukuk … As at earlier this year, the remaining outstanding amount [of the sukuk] was only RM150 million. We pre-repaid them as our cash flow was comfortable.”  With most of its debts cleared, local rating agency RAM upgraded Country Garden Malaysia’s outlook rating from negative to stable in March, reflecting its balance-sheet resilience despite global sector volatility.  That financial stability has been supported by developments on the legal front. Malaysian courts have recently upheld the validity of sales and purchase agreements in favour of the developer. Dismissing buyer suits seeking to void contracts for reasons such as media portrayals of the project as a “ghost town”, the courts established that market downturns and post-purchase regret do not constitute grounds for breach. The decisions shield CGPV against speculative contract cancellations and protect its revenue base.  “Forest City has completed and delivered 26,000 residential units so far. We understand that we cannot make every single person happy, and it is normal to receive feedback or complaints. We respect the buyers’ legal rights,” Li says.  “But we also have our internal KPIs [key performance indicators] to meet. We are pleased to share that customer satisfaction consistently hits above 95% in our surveys and polls. Generally, the majority of our 20,000 residents are happy to live here, or they wouldn’t choose to continue staying. This is evidenced by our growing population.”  A city waking up  Today, Forest City is home to around 20,000 people living in 66 completed blocks, over 770 acres of the approved 5,000-acre reclaimed island land bank.  “If you pass by from Iskandar Puteri towards Batam, you can see the lights on across the residential towers at night,” Syarul says. “It is a night-and-day difference compared with what people experienced immediately after the pandemic in early 2021.”  Demographics have shifted significantly, he adds. While buyers were once predominantly mainland Chinese, the current resident base is largely local Malaysians, many of whom commute daily to Singapore or work in nearby industrial parks, as well as expatriates of different nationalities.  “The township’s commercial pulse is also quickening,” says Syarul. “The Fisherman’s Wharf commercial street has seen steady footfall, with duty-free shops, eateries and premier banking facilities, including branches of Maybank and CIMB, with Affin Bank and AmBank joining the fold soon.”  Forest City attracts between 1.5 million and two million tourists annually. Its crown jewel is Forest City Golf Resort, located on the mainland about 9km from the man-made islands. Featuring two 18-hole international championship courses, it draws golfers from Japan, South Korea and Singapore.  There is also an affordable beachfront water park that offers weekend entertainment for visiting families.  “Forest City is probably the only sandy beach in Johor Bahru. Otherwise, you have to go to Desaru, which is an hour away. To draw more visitors, we are also collaborating with some watersports academies on courses for adults and children. The beach and water park are very popular during school holidays and weekends, contributing to our growing annual tourist and visitor numbers,” Syarul says.  Meanwhile, Network School, a start-up society and experimental community based on Silicon Valley entrepreneur Balaji Srinivasan’s book The Network State, was set up in the township in October 2024.  Balaji’s private co-living and co-working hub at Marina Hotel drew hundreds of international digital nomads, crypto enthusiasts and tech workers.  However, in July 2026, the Iskandar Puteri City Council (MBIP) revoked the Network School operator’s business licence for breaching local licensing conditions. The management of the school clarified that CGPV operates solely as a commercial landlord, and that the developer is fully cooperating with the local authorities to ensure all commercial tenants adhere to the regulatory framework.  Strategic shift  Li says while Forest City’s master plan is unchanged, CGPV is shifting its focus towards commercial and industrial developments, in alignment with the government’s broader economic development plan for the state.  “We maintain the master plan as it is because, to us, it is still a very fantastic plan even after a decade. Of course, for such a mega development, you have to do it in phases, and there will be small twists and adjustments in between. But overall, we do not have plans to review the master plan. Now, we are embarking on the third phase of development. We foresee the entire master plan being completed only by 2040. It is now 12% to 13% developed,” says Syarul.  The biggest “twists and adjustments” to the master plan were its integration into the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) and designation as an SFZ.  In August 2023, the government announced that Forest City would be designated as an SFZ to boost foreign investment, with incentives such as a 15% income tax rate for skilled workers and lower business operating costs. A year later, the government launched the tax incentive framework for the SFZ, which includes a zero tax rate for single family offices (SFO), a 5% corporate tax rate for fintech and global business services, and concessionary income tax rates.  In early 2025, Malaysia and Singapore signed a bilateral agreement to establish the JS-SEZ. Under the agreement, Forest City was formally incorporated as Flagship G, one of nine primary flagship zones within the 3,505 sq km economic zone.  “We started [the master plan] with residential and, maybe, this made people misunderstand that Forest City is focusing on high-rise residential developments. The SFZ designation puts us right back on track to [industrial projects],” says Li.  “Under the SFZ blueprint, the development is divided into two distinct functional zones, where the island component acts as a core financial services hub, focusing on single-family offices, fintech, foreign payment operating systems and back-office financial services. Meanwhile, the mainland focuses on smart logistics, high-tech manufacturing and global business services.”  To encourage direct investments in Forest City, the Malaysian government established the Iskandar Malaysia Facilitation Centre Johor (IMFC-J) at Forest City’s 42-storey primary office tower, Menara Delima Satu, to streamline the investment process. The centre houses 18 government agencies under one roof and acts as a single processing point for foreign investors.  “A key cornerstone of the SFZ is attracting family offices. The SC (Securities Commission) set an AUM (assets under management) threshold of RM30 million for family offices setting up in Forest City, a far more accessible entry point compared with Singapore’s S$15 million (RM47.9 million) requirement or Hong Kong’s HK$240 million (RM124.7 million) benchmark,” Li says.  Syarul stresses, however, that Malaysia is not competing with Singapore or Hong Kong in the SFO segment but is instead complementing them.  “It is about synergy. Under the SFZ rules, family offices in Forest City can invest up to 90% of their AUM globally. This means that investors can set up their operational base here in Forest City at one-third to one-fourth of the operational cost, while still leveraging Singapore’s capital markets just across the strait. It is very attractive to many family offices,” he explains.  Under the SFO Incentive Scheme guidelines issued by the SC, it is mandatory to establish a physical office in Forest City to qualify for and maintain SC approval and the accompanying 0% tax incentive.  According to Li, over 40 SFOs have secured physi­cal office space in Forest City, with nine having formally received SC approval to date.  “We are very positive about this, though we do not have an actual target of having many of them in Forest City in the near future because it is beyond our control and SC has its plan. But it is a strong catalyst in helping to add vibrancy to Forest City because when the offices come, they bring in their professional teams — accountants, lawyers and finance and investment experts,” he adds.  Forest City is also targeting global business services. CGPV is in advanced discussions with two major international banking institutions — one looking to relocate its back-office operations from Singapore, and another expanding its operational footprint from Kuala Lumpur.  Forest City 2.0  Despite the tailwinds from the SFZ, Li and Syarul acknowledge that transforming the mega project into a self-sustaining regional economy is not without immediate, real-world hurdles. The most pressing challenge currently is cross-border physical connectivity and accessibility.  “While the project is geographically proximate to Singapore, seamlessly moving people, goods and daily commuters across borders remains a complex, multi-jurisdictional effort,” says Li. “Furthermore, regional competition from peers like Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam means that Malaysia must continually sharpen its execution speed and policy delivery to stay ahead.”  To close this connectivity gap, Country Garden is taking interim measures while lobbying government authorities for long-term infrastructure approvals.  “Before all the major government infrastructure projects are completed, we are bridging the gap ourselves. We currently run daily direct shuttles transferring residents and workers to the Sultan Abu Bakar CIQ Second Link complex,” Li says.  For the long term, the developer has submitted plans to the joint Malaysia-Singapore ministerial committee under the Iskandar Regional Development Authority (IRDA) for a dedicated ferry terminal. Once approved, ferry routes will connect Forest City directly to Raffles Marina in Singapore and Batam in Indonesia.  “We are also asking the government for assistance to permit a direct highway connection linking straight to Tuas, and to integrate Forest City into upcoming regional rail routes like the RTS [Rapid Transit System], ART [Automated Rapid Transit] and transport corridors heading to Kulai and Senai,” he adds. “Moving people efficiently is crucial to unlocking the full value of the JS-SEZ but because these are country-to-country matters, we have to keep pushing and following up continuously.”  Simultaneously, the master developer is pivoting to boosting population density and creating high-value local jobs, away from traditional residential property sales, towards what the team calls “Forest City 2.0”.  “We are not launching any more residential projects in the near future, but focusing on clearing the inventory. We will advance commercial and industrial land development earlier than originally scheduled to inject immediate economic vibrancy,” Li says. “Our next focus is to bring in companies and industries to invest or establish their presence here.”  Acknowledging the importance of generating sufficient jobs to increase Forest City’s population, CGPV is actively trying to draw data centres, logistics players and manufacturers to its upcoming 418-acre industrial park.  “We need to create real economic dynamics. If you don’t generate jobs and economic substance, you cannot sustain a population,” Li stresses.  The response to this industrial shift has been positive. In the first half of this year alone, the developer logged over 300 company enquiries and secured a 40-acre industrial land deal with a manufacturer in Phase 1 of the industrial park, paving the way for ready-built factory developments in Phase 2 should market demand sustain.  In another strategic partnership, Country Garden recently signed a term sheet with Penang-based Oriental Holdings Bhd (KL: ORIENT) to develop a RM750 million healthcare hub in Forest City, anchored by a 500-bed hospital alongside comprehensive medical supply chain services.  “Internationally, we are actively introducing Forest City to big-name [multinational corporations]. It is not so much for their name, but the entire supply chain. We are looking to bring in ‘queen bee’ investors,” Li says. “We have been doing roadshows, especially in China, to introduce the JS-SEZ and Forest City SFZ. We went to Shenzhen and Suzhou, which have some of the most successful industrial parks in China.”  Apart from the industrial park, CGPV has also received enquiries from international investors interested in private island parcels.  “It is something that we are looking at. Instead of standard residential towers, we can custom-reclaim approved island plots, such as 1.5 to two acres, based entirely on an investor’s specific operational or residential requirements. It’s about being adaptive to what the current market actually demands,” he says.  Road to 2030 and beyond  Apart from Forest City, Country Garden Malaysia has four other major developments in Johor and the Klang Valley, executed largely through JVs.  “Out of our five projects in Malaysia, four are structured as JVs,” Li explains. “Only Danga Bay is 100% held by Country Garden Malaysia. We welcome JVs because local partners bring value to the table, though for master site design, we prefer to lead.”  In Johor Bahru, Country Garden Central Park has completed three phases comprising over 3,000 residential units that are nearly fully sold. The developer is now planning subsequent sub-phases over a 10- to 12-year development cycle.  In Kuala Lumpur, the initial two phases of township development Lake City in Taman Wahyu are completed and sold out, with Phase 3 scheduled for launch next year. The remaining four parcels have been earmarked for development over a 15-year period.  In Semenyih, Selangor, residential development Diamond City launched its final landed parcel in September 2025, which is expected to wrap up construction within two years.  With a substantial land bank in its existing portfolio, the developer will focus its resources on executing its active pipeline over the next decade.  As the interview draws to a close, both Li and Syarul reflect on the long-term nature of master township development.  “Rome was not built in a day,” Li says. “When we first came to this coastal area in Johor, it was completely rural. Today, the infrastructure is firmly established. Development never moves in a straight upward line; it moves in spirals, but it always moves forward.  “We wish the public to know that since the first day Country Garden has been here in Malaysia, we have wanted to be here long term. Of course, there are twists and turns over the years, but we cannot deny the contribution of the company in Malaysia.”  He says Country Garden has invested RM32 billion in Malaysia, including RM20 billion in Forest City alone.  “We have created jobs, contributed to the country’s tax revenues and trained local skilled workers. Most importantly, after so many challenges and uncertainties, we were here, and we are still here today. The fundamentals are in place, and we have absolute faith in what Forest City will become.”

title: 'Monday wrap: Young architects rise, insurers rethink adequacy, AI trust gaps widen
body: 'Architecture's young talent, a shift in insurance strategy, AI trust gaps, and rising bank margins mark the week.  Last week in Singapore Business Review, eight architects under 40 were named for their work on hospitals, civic infrastructure, and heritage projects. Etiqa Insurance said the industry's challenge is shifting from expanding coverage to ensuring adequacy as customers plan for retirement and wealth transfer. Nearly all IT leaders reported artificial intelligence (AI) tools accessing sensitive data without permission, whilst AI shopping adoption climbed even as checkout trust lagged. Banks, meanwhile, are expected to see margins rise as SORA climbs toward 1.4% by year-end.  Singapore Business Review's list of notable architecture professionals under 40 for 2026 features eight honourees—five women and three men—from DP Architects, SAA Architects, RSP Architects Planners & Engineers, CPG Consultants, and Chang Architects. Their combined portfolio spans a $790m hotel (the largest Mercure property worldwide), Singapore's first fully integrated healthcare campus at Woodlands Hospital, and civic landmarks including One Punggol's Regional Library and the Goh Keng Swee Centre for Education, a 30-storey office tower under active construction.  Standout work included Kelvin Ng Si Hoa's role delivering Woodlands Hospital despite expressway noise and rocky terrain constraints, and Loh Zhu Ping's contributions to the $450m Funan Redevelopment and the $790m Mercure ICON Singapore City Centre.  Singapore insurers should shift focus from expanding coverage to ensuring policy adequacy, according to Etiqa Insurance Singapore CEO Claudia Soh, as customers increasingly treat insurance as part of long-term financial planning rather than pure protection against loss. Singapore's insurance penetration stood at 7.6% of GDP as of May 2026, ranking fourth among selected Asian markets behind South Korea, Taiwan, and Hong Kong.  A May CIMB report found 52.6% of residents viewed insurance as supporting financial independence, up from 45% in 2025, with customers increasingly looking at retirement, wealth-building, and inheritance planning. Soh said AI can help insurers tailor services but cautioned that "trust, human judgement, and meaningful customer relationships remain just as important."  Nearly all Singaporean IT leaders (98.9%) reported an AI tool or agent accessing sensitive data beyond its intended scope in the past year, the second-highest rate among eight markets surveyed in Delinea's 2026 Identity Security Report.  Despite 99.6% of organisations having a formal AI data access policy, only 14% of IT leaders can detect a scope violation as it happens, and 72% take a full day or longer to catch one—the highest globally. Employee behaviour compounds the risk: 84% of Singaporean employees said they have bypassed required approval processes for AI use, and just 38% of IT leaders said they can always trace a sensitive access event back to a named human authoriser.  Singapore consumers are increasingly shopping with AI, but remain wary of letting it complete purchases, according to Adyen's 2026 Singapore Retail Report. Whilst 72% of consumers use AI assistants for shopping, only 29% are comfortable letting AI complete a purchase, and 49% of existing AI shopping users hesitate at the payment stage.  Still, AI-referred visitors generate 53% more revenue per visit and convert 54% more than non-AI traffic. Separately, Salesforce's State of Commerce report found 82% of Singapore commerce leaders expect large language models to become essential to product discovery within the year, with agentic search usage as a shopping-journey starting point up 200% year-over-year.  Singapore's three-month benchmark borrowing rate is expected to climb to 1.4% by year-end, supporting bank margins into 2027, according to UOB Kay Hian. The three-month compounded SORA rose to 1.22% in the third quarter after falling to 1.02% in April, reflecting MAS's tighter monetary policy stance amid slowing money supply growth.  UOB Kay Hian raised its 2027 net profit forecasts for DBS and OCBC by 5.7% and 4.7% respectively, citing expected margin gains, whilst flagging risks from elevated US rates and potential Red Sea shipping disruptions that could push freight and oil costs higher.

title: 'A pay rise for only half the workforce
body: 'Lim Guan Eng was the first senior politicians to call for migrant workers in micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to be exempt from the minimum wage and Employees Provident Fund (EPF) schemes. Now, the cabinet has exempted MSMEs from the upcoming minimum wage increase “for the time being”. The entrepreneur development and cooperatives minister, also from the DAP, announced the decision. Syabas (well done) on this remarkable ‘achievement’. Millions of workers in the sector have lost their right to a minimum wage increase. Official figures show about 48.7% of the country’s total employment are in MSMEs. That is 8.1 million people. Can Malaysia ever become a high-income nation with so many workers exempt from the minimum wake hike? We should also worry that wages will stay stagnant. Wage growth for 8.1 million workers will probably be held back. Two classes of workers Almost half of those workers will benefit from a higher minimum wage. The other half will, regrettably, be left at the mercy of their bosses for any wage reviews. This is discrimination in how we treat our workers. Even the government of the day never envisaged such injustice when it introduced the policy. The minimum wage was meant to set a floor for all workers. Since 2013, the government has never strayed from that core aim. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member Now, under the supposedly caring ‘Madani’ government, low-wage workers are being treated unfairly to favour one class of employers. It is a case of “harapkan pagar, pagar makan padi”. Some businesses will feel the impact of a higher minimum wage. The government should address their concerns case by case, rather than excluding the whole MSME sector. Denying close to 8.1m workers coverage under the new minimum wage increase is deeply unjust and morally wrong. We call on the prime minister to reverse the decision to exempt MSMEs from the upcoming minimum wage increase. title: 'Are Chinese Malaysian-owned SMEs being ‘killed’ by the China onslaught?
body: 'The Gut Shot Podcast is joined by its geopolitical and economic consultant to governments and companies, Jason Leong. Signals from the ground have now raised alarm among segments of the Chinese Malaysian community. Malaysia’s private sector economy is largely driven by local ethnic Chinese businesses. Unlike the ecosystem of government-linked firms and investment companies, the private sector economy has none of the protection that bumiputra monopolies and oligopolies enjoy. The retail, mechanic workshops, construction services and supply chains, food and beverage and other service businesses are not abstract figures on an economist’s spreadsheet. They are livelihoods that have survived for decades. They have employed workers, paid taxes, supported families and funded the education of the next generation. Now a wave of imported competition from China, at scaled-down and even cut-throat prices, has reached our shores with devastating effect. When businesses across very different sectors begin telling the same story at the same time (vanishing margins, slowing customers, rising costs, price competition that cannot be met and a daily struggle to survive), we should not dismiss it as a series of isolated failures or a lack of competitiveness. This podcast explores the damage to local ethnic Chinese-driven small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in both macro and micro terms, calmly and without sentiment and makes some policy recommendations. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member It examines why, however efficient our supply chains become, resistance on scale alone will be futile: massive state subsidies, fierce internal competition within China that no other country can replicate, and a capital structure built to chase market share at any cost. The official macro numbers may not have captured this yet. Perhaps no one has measured it properly or raised the alarm. But the signals are real. By the time everyone agrees there is a crisis, many of these businesses could already be gone. If we fail to recognise the systemic forces behind China’s global dominance and act accordingly, we may be witnessing the beginning of the end of the traditional, generations-old Chinese Malaysian SMEs ecosystem. This podcast explores the damage to local ethnic Chinese-driven small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in both macro and micro terms, calmly and without sentiment and makes some policy recommendations. - Sign up for Aliran's free daily email updates or weekly newsletters or both - Make a one-off donation to Persatuan Aliran Kesedaran Negara (ALIRAN), Maybank a/c 507246118995 or CIMB a/c 8004240948 - Make a regular pledge or periodic auto-donation to Aliran - Become an Aliran member It examines why, however efficient our supply chains become, resistance on scale alone will be futile: massive state subsidies, fierce internal competition within China that no other country can replicate, and a capital structure built to chase market share at any cost. The official macro numbers may not have captured this yet. Perhaps no one has measured it properly or raised the alarm. But the signals are real. By the time everyone agrees there is a crisis, many of these businesses could already be gone. If we fail to recognise the systemic forces behind China’s global dominance and act accordingly, we may be witnessing the beginning of the end of the traditional, generations-old Chinese Malaysian SMEs ecosystem. title: 'High Court issues arrest warrant for accused in Palestinian abduction case
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR: The High Court today issued an arrest warrant for an accused in the 2022 abduction of a Palestinian man after he failed to appear for pre-trial case management. Judge Datuk Mohd Arief Emran Arifin issued the warrant against Muhammad Iqmal Abdul Rahis, 31, the seventh of eight accused, after allowing an application by deputy public prosecutor Zaileen Nadia Zubir. During the proceedings, Zaileen told the court that Iqmal had been uncontactable since Sept 11 and that his bailor had lodged a police report. The judge then asked the bailor to explain the situation. She told the court that she had gone to Iqmal's house to look for him but was unable to locate him. "I also went to his village in Tanjung Sepat, Kuala Langat, in Selangor and even searched a nearby oil palm plantation. "However, even his siblings did not know his whereabouts. "That prompted me to lodge a police report on his disappearance," she said. Zaileen also said police had gone to Tanjung Sepat to interview Iqmal's parents about his whereabouts. "Police investigations showed that his father said his son had not returned to the village since January. Efforts to trace him are still ongoing," she said. In addition to issuing the arrest warrant, Arief Emran ordered the RM50,000 bail to be returned to the bailor after hearing that she had made efforts to locate Iqmal. Iqmal was represented by lawyer Goh Cia Yee. The other seven accused, who are out on bail, were present in court today. They are Tengku Arif Bongsu Tengku Hamid, 45; Mohamad Naziree Mustapha, 45; Faizull Hardey Mohd Isa, 46; Mohd Zaidi Mohd Zain, 60; Nidarahayu Zainal, 40; Raibafie Amdan, 45; and Edy Ko'im Said, 46. The court had previously fixed the trial for Oct 12 to 15, Oct 19 to 23, and Oct 26 to 29. In October 2022, 13 men and a woman were charged at the magistrate's court here with abducting Palestinian Omar ZM Albelbaisy Raeda, 35, allegedly to obtain a reward in the form of information relating to software used to hack mobile phones. They were Edy Ko'im, 45; Mohamad Norakmal Hassan, 46; Dody Junaidi, 47; Tengku Arif Bongsu Tengku Hamid, 44; Mohamad Naziree Mustapha, 44; Faizull Hardey Mohd Isa, 45; Muhammad Iqmal, 30; Mohamad Sufian Saly, 28; Muhammad Al Hatim; Nidarahayu Zainal, 39; Raibafie Amdan, 44; Mohd Zaidi Mohd Zain, 59; Mohd Azwan Jamaludin, 42; and Tengku Hazarul Ismail Tengku Hamid, 54. They were charged with committing the offence at Jalan Mayang here about 10.40pm on Sept 28, 2022. The charge was framed under Section 3 of the Kidnapping Act 1961, read together with Section 34 of the Penal Code, which carries a jail term of between 30 and 40 years and whipping upon conviction. On Oct 20, 2023, Tengku Arif Bongsu, together with married couple Nidarahayu and Raibafie, were also charged with 19 counts of money laundering involving more than RM250,000. For the first to fourth charges, Nidarahayu was accused of disposing of RM20,650.86 in proceeds from unlawful activity from her savings account at CIMB Bank into two other bank accounts at CIMB Bank and Maybank Islamic Bhd's Taman Maluri branch between Sept 15 and Oct 3, 2022. She also faced 13 charges of transferring RM184,985.46 into the accounts of four companies and eight individuals, also allegedly proceeds from unlawful activity, between Sept 15 and Oct 2 that year. Raibafie and Tengku Arif Bongsu were respectively charged with receiving RM30,350 and RM25,000 from two bank accounts belonging to Nidarahayu and a company at CIMB Bank's Jalan Bukit Bintang and Taman Mutiara, Cheras branches between Sept 29 and Oct 2, 2022. The charges were framed under Section 4(1)(b) of the Anti-Money Laundering, Anti-Terrorism Financing and Proceeds of Unlawful Activities Act 2001, which carries a maximum 15-year jail term and a fine of five times the value of the unlawful activity or RM5 million, whichever is higher, upon conviction. On July 10, 2025, six men were sentenced to five years in jail by the High Court here after pleading guilty to an alternative charge of forcibly taking and confining the victim. Judge K. Muniandy, who is now a Court of Appeal judge, imposed the sentence on Mohamad Norakmal, Mohd Azwan, Dody, Mohamad Sufian, Tengku Hazarul Ismail and Muhammad Al Hatim. According to the charge, they were accused of forcibly taking the victim and wrongfully and secretly confining him at Jalan Mayang, Dang Wangi, here, at 10.40pm on Sept 28, 2022. All six were charged under Section 365 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 34, which carries a jail term of up to seven years and a fine. According to the facts of the case, the victim was abducted and confined at a chalet in Hulu Langat. A police raid, carried out based on information received, led to the victim's rescue. He was found with his hands and legs tied with cable ties.

title: 'Warga Palestin diculik: Waran tangkap terhadap tertuduh ketujuh
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR – Mahkamah Tinggi di sini pada Jumaat mengeluarkan waran tangkap terhadap seorang daripada lapan tertuduh dalam kes penculikan seorang lelaki warga Palestin pada 2022. Hakim, Datuk Mohd Arief Emran Arifin mengeluarkan perintah itu terhadap Muhammad Iqmal Abdul Rahis, 31, selepas tertuduh tidak hadir pada prosiding kes berkenaan. Ketika pengurusan kes, penjamin tertuduh memaklumkan bahawa, usaha menjejaki Muhammad Iqmal termasuk pergi ke rumahnya di kawasan ladang kelapa sawit telah dilakukan sebelum ini. “Saya pergi ke kampungnya di Tanjung Sepat, tetapi adik-beradik dia kata tidak jumpa,” katanya. Sementara itu, Timbalan Pendakwa Raya, Zaileen Nadia Zubir berkata, pihak pendakwaan juga sudah berusaha mengesan tertuduh ketujuh itu sejak 11 September lalu. Menurutnya, pihak berkuasa turut pergi ke Tanjung Sepat, Banting, Kuala Langan dan bertanyakan mengenai keberadaan tertuduh kepada bapanya. “Bapa tertuduh memberitahu lelaki berkenaan tidak balik kampung sejak Januari lalu dan pihak berkuasa masih berusaha mengesan tertuduh,” katanya. Susulan itu, Hakim, Mohd Arief Emran mengeluarkan waran tangkap terhadap Muhammad Iqmal. Mahkamah turut memerintahkan wang jaminan sebanyak RM50,000 dikembalikan kepada penjamin selepas mengambil kira usaha yang dilakukan bagi mengesan tertuduh. Dalam prosiding itu, Muhammad Iqmal diwakili peguam, Goh Cia Yee. Sebelum ini, mahkamah menetapkan perbicaraan kes berkenaan ditetapkan pada 12 hingga 15, 19 hingga 23 dan 26 hingga 29 October. Pada Oktober 2022, seramai 13 lelaki dan seorang wanita didakwa di Mahkamah Majistret di sini atas pertuduhan menculik warga Palestin, Omar Z M Albelbaisy Raeda, 35, bagi mendapatkan ganjaran berupa rahsia maklumat berkaitan perisian menggodam telefon bimbit. Mereka ialah Edy Ko’im Said, 46, Mohamad Norakmal Hassan, 47, Dody Junaidi, 48, Tengku Arif Bongsu Tengku Hamid, 45, Mohamad Naziree Mustapha, 45, Faizull Hardey Mohd Isa, 46, Muhammad Iqmal, Mohamad Sufian Saly, 29, Muhammad Al Hatim Mohd Fauzi, 29, Nidarahayu Zainal, 40, Raibafie Amdan, 45, Mohd Zaidi Mohd Zain, 60, Mohd Azwan Jamaludin 55, dan Tengku Hazarul Ismail Tengku Hamid, 55. Kesalahan itu didakwa dilakukan di Jalan Mayang, di sini, pada jam 10.40 malam 28 September 2022. Pertuduhan dibuat mengikut Seksyen 3 Akta Penculikan 1961 dibaca bersama Seksyen 34 Kanun Keseksaan yang memperuntukkan hukuman penjara antara 30 hingga 40 tahun serta sebatan, jika sabit kesalahan. Pada 20 Oktober 2023, Tengku Arif Bongsu bersama pasangan suami isteri, Nidarahayu dan Raibafie turut didakwa atas 19 pertuduhan pengubahan wang haram berjumlah lebih RM250,000. Bagi pertuduhan pertama hingga keempat, Nidarahayu didakwa melupuskan wang RM20,650.86 hasil aktiviti haram daripada akaun simpanannya di CIMB Bank ke dua akaun bank lain di CIMB Bank dan Maybank Islamic Berhad di Cawangan Taman Maluri, antara 15 September hingga 3 Oktober 2022. Dia turut berdepan 13 pertuduhan memindahkan wang RM184,985.46 ke dalam akaun empat syarikat dan lapan individu, juga hasil aktiviti haram, antara 15 September hingga 2 Oktober tahun sama. Raibafie dan Tengku Arif Bongsu masing-masing didakwa menerima RM30,350 dan RM25,000 daripada dua akaun bank milik Nidarahayu serta sebuah syarikat, di CIMB Bank Cawangan Jalan Bukit Bintang dan Taman Mutiara, Cheras antara 29 September hingga 2 Oktober 2022. Pertuduhan dibuat mengikut Seksyen 4(1)(b) Akta Pencegahan Pengubahan Wang Haram, Pencegahan Pembiayaan Keganasan dan Hasil daripada Aktiviti Haram 2001 yang membawa hukuman penjara maksimum 15 tahun dan denda lima kali ganda nilai aktiviti haram atau RM5 juta, yang mana lebih tinggi, jika sabit kesalahan. Pada 10 Julai 2025, enam lelaki dihukum penjara lima tahun oleh Mahkamah Tinggi di sini selepas mengaku bersalah atas pertuduhan pilihan melarikan dan mengurung seorang lelaki Palestin itu. Hakim, K Muniandy yang kini hakim Mahkamah Rayuan di Putrajaya, menjatuhkan hukuman itu terhadap Mohamad Norakmal, Mohd Azwan, Dody, Mohamad Sufian, Tengku Hazarul Ismail dan Muhammad Al Hatim. Mengikut pertuduhan, mereka didakwa melarikan mangsa secara paksa terhadap lelaki Palestine sama dengan dikurung secara salah dan rahsia di Jalan Mayang, Dang Wangi di sini pada jam 10.40 malam, 28 September 2022. Kesemua tertuduh didakwa mengikut Seksyen 365 Kanun Keseksaan dan dibaca bersama Seksyen 34 akta sama yang membawa hukuman penjara sehingga tujuh tahun dan boleh dikenakan denda. Mengikut fakta kes, mangsa dilarikan dan dikurung di sebuah chalet di Hulu Langat. Serbuan polis yang dilakukan berdasarkan maklumat berjaya menyelamatkan mangsa yang ketika itu berada dalam keadaan tangan dan kaki diikat dengan pengikat kabel.

title: 'Ibu janji nak ambil dari sekolah, tapi dia pergi selamanya'
body: 'Gua Musang: Hancur hati dua beradik apabila ibu yang dinanti untuk menjemput pulang dari sekolah tidak kunjung tiba, sebaliknya berita duka diterima apabila insan tersayang itu meninggal dunia akibat kemalangan. Nur Arissa Najla Mohd Shazuam, 13, dan Nur Amani Nuwairah Mohd Shazuam, 15, menanti penuh sabar selepas ibunya, Nor Hasyikim Daud, 34, berjanji untuk mengambilnya pulang dari sekolah di Sekolah Menengah Kebangsaan (SMK) Bandar Chiku. Nur Arissa Najla berkata, dia menerima berita ibunya kemalangan daripada seorang rakan pada jam 1.40 tengah hari. Katanya, ketika itu dia bersama kakak sedang menunggu ibunya yang berjanji untuk mengambil mereka pulang dari sekolah. "Ibu ada maklumkan akan ke Bandar Gua Musang dengan rakannya dan berjanji mengambil saya dan kakak dari sekolah. "Pada hari kejadian, saya menduduki tiga kertas peperiksaan dan sangat teruja untuk memberitahu ibu yang saya boleh jawab semua soalan subjek Sejarah. "Lebih setengah jam menanti ibu namun tidak kunjung tiba, sebaliknya saya terima berita ibu kemalangan. "Ketika itu juga saya nampak bapa saudara datang untuk menjemput kami," katanya ketika ditemui di Felda Chiku 5, di sini. Dalam kejadian pada Ahad lalu Nor Hasyikim maut di lokasi kejadian apabila kenderaan Produa Axia yang dipandunya bertembung dengan sebuah lori 10 tan di Kilometer 40 Jalan Gua Musang-Kuala Krai. Mangsa maut di lokasi kejadian akibat tersepit manakala rakannya yang berada di tempat duduk penumpang hadapan mengalami kecederaan parah. Selain Nur Arissa Najla dan Nur Amani Nuwairah, arwah turut meninggalkan seorang bayi Nur Aireen Nisrina yang berusia 11 bulan. Sementara itu, kakak kepada Nor Hasyikim, Siti Noraeshah Daud, 39, berkata, tiga beradik itu akan dijaga oleh ibunya dengan bantuan adik beradik lain. "Sejak setahun lalu arwah membesarkan tiga anaknya dengan bekerja di kantin asrama SMK Bandar Chiku. "Selepas ini kami akan bersama-sama menjaga dan membesarkan tiga anak perempuan arwah," katanya. Orang ramai yang ingin memberi sumbangan boleh menyalurkan ke akaun Bank CIMB milik Siti Noraeshah Daud bernombor 7601845122.

"Ketika itu juga saya nampak bapa saudara datang untuk menjemput kami," katanya ketika ditemui di Felda Chiku 5, di sini. Dalam kejadian pada Ahad lalu Nor Hasyikim maut di lokasi kejadian apabila kenderaan Produa Axia yang dipandunya bertembung dengan sebuah lori 10 tan di Kilometer 40 Jalan Gua Musang-Kuala Krai. Mangsa maut di lokasi kejadian akibat tersepit manakala rakannya yang berada di tempat duduk penumpang hadapan mengalami kecederaan parah. Selain Nur Arissa Najla dan Nur Amani Nuwairah, arwah turut meninggalkan seorang bayi Nur Aireen Nisrina yang berusia 11 bulan. Sementara itu, kakak kepada Nor Hasyikim, Siti Noraeshah Daud, 39, berkata, tiga beradik itu akan dijaga oleh ibunya dengan bantuan adik beradik lain. "Sejak setahun lalu arwah membesarkan tiga anaknya dengan bekerja di kantin asrama SMK Bandar Chiku. "Selepas ini kami akan bersama-sama menjaga dan membesarkan tiga anak perempuan arwah," katanya. Orang ramai yang ingin memberi sumbangan boleh menyalurkan ke akaun Bank CIMB milik Siti Noraeshah Daud bernombor 7601845122.

title: 'HLIB Retail Research – Tradersbrief 23 Sep
body: 'Global. Asian markets ended mixed as investors weighed easing oil prices and bond yields against lingering geopolitical risks. Sentiment remained cautious ahead of the 23–25 Sep Trump-Xi meeting, with markets hoping for an extension of the US-China trade truce while watching developments on AI, export controls and rare-earth supplies. Meanwhile, Iran indicated it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure, while Saudi Arabia reportedly restarted its East-West Pipeline, raising hopes of improving oil supply. Wall Street (Dow -0.36%, S&P 500 0.0%, Nasdaq 0.45%) ended mixed as continued AI strength offset weakness in financials, while easing oil prices and geopolitical tensions supported sentiment. AI infrastructure stocks remained in demand, fuelled by strong reception for Meta’s Muse AI agent. Meanwhile, Anthropic’s new lower-cost AI model added to optimism over broader AI adoption, with its reported IPO targeted for November. Geopolitical risks remained in focus as Trump said the US and Iran could reach a deal after the November midterm elections, while Tehran indicated it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if Washington eased military pressure. Malaysia. Tracking Wall Street gains, bargain-hunting in selected heavyweights and oversold readings, the KLCI jumped 16.6 pts to 1,683.5, led by IHH, CIMB, SUNWAY, HLBANK, PBBANK and MAYBANK. Market breadth improved to 1.48 from 1.18, while trading activity rose 5% to 3.58bn shares worth RM3.15bn. Foreign institutions (+RM20m; 5D: +RM75m; MTD: -RM674m; YTD: -RM5.13bn) and local retailers (+RM20m; 5D: +RM205m; MTD: +RM1.06bn; YTD: +RM0.62bn) were net buyers, while local institutions remained net sellers (-RM40m; 5D: -RM280m; MTD: -RM389m; YTD: +RM4.51bn). After a 95-pt surge from its YTD low of 1,655 on 29 Jun to 1,753 on 26 Aug, the KLCI corrected to 1,661.9 (21 Sep) before rebounding to 1,683.5 on 22 Sep, with momentum indicators turning up. However, the index remains below the LT ascending line and within the descending channel, keeping the near-term bias bearish, with major supports pegged at 1,655 (YTD low) and 1,639 (23.6% FR). On the upside, reclaiming 1,685 (50% FR) and 1,701 (MA200) would strengthen signs of stabilisation, targeting 1,717 (MA50) and 1,731 (76.4% FR). A decisive breakout above these levels would negate the bearish setup and refocus attention on 1,753 and 1,771 (YTD high). With expectations of a constructive Trump-Xi summit, easing oil prices and oversold technical readings, the KLCI could extend its rebound towards 1,700. However, the index remains entrenched in a downtrend channel, while tricky domestic backdrops—including potential 2H earnings disappointments amid a higher-for-longer cost environment, the dissolution of the Melaka state assembly today for the 16th state election, and lingering GE16 speculation—could cap gains and keep volatility elevated ahead of Budget 2027 on 9 Oct. title: 'ViTrox Hits New Record High as AI-driven Growth Boosts Outlook
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR (Sept 22): Shares in ViTrox Corporation Bhd (KL:VITROX) hit their highest level since the company’s listing on the ACE Market in 2005 on Tuesday, driven by its strong growth prospects amid the AI infrastructure boom. ViTrox designs & manufactures vision inspection system & handler for back-end semiconductor industry. In a The Edge Malaysia weekly’s Sept 21-Sept 27 issue, its co-founder and managing director Datuk Chu Jenn Weng said the company’s numbers will double this year, with strong growth momentum expected to continue over the next few years. The Penang-based automated test equipment maker’s shares charted an all-time high of RM10.08 before closing up 21 sen or 2.2% at RM10 on Tuesday, giving the company a market capitalisation of a little under RM19 billion. The share price remains below the consensus 12-month target price of RM10.67, while the highest 12-month target price is RM13. The majority of analysts covering the company have a “buy” call on the stock, with 11 “buy” calls, two “hold” calls and one “sell” call. Analysts noted that ViTrox has positioned itself as a key beneficiary of AI infrastructure spending. Research houses have also upgraded their earnings forecasts, with Apex Securities raising its net profit forecasts for FY2026, FY2027 and FY2028 to RM275.6 million, RM362.4 million and RM408.2 million, respectively, citing sustained AI infrastructure demand. CIMB Securities noted that ViTrox’s 1HFY2026 results exceeded expectations, coming in at more than 60% of its full-year consensus estimate. The research house reiterated its “buy” rating with a target price of RM10.00 and raised its FY2026–FY2028 earnings per share estimates by 28% to 37%, citing expanding order books, a favourable product mix and recurring service income. ViTrox saw its revenue double year-on-year in the second quarter ended June 30 (2QFY2026) to RM375 million from RM183 million in the same period last year. Net profit for the quarter jumped to RM85.04 million, bringing the company’s cumulative net profit for the first half of 2026 to RM136.24 million, surpassing its full-year net profit of RM133.18 million in 2025. Chu said the optimism surrounding the company is understandable, given that, much like its peers in the semiconductor-related industry, ViTrox is operating at full capacity and expanding to cope with the surge in demand. title: 'FBM KLCI Susut 15 Mata, Saham Bank & Utiliti Tekan Pasaran
body: 'Bursa Malaysia meneruskan penurunan pada tengah hari Khamis apabila tekanan jualan kembali mendominasi pasaran, selari dengan prestasi bercampur pasaran global ketika kenaikan hasil bon Perbendaharaan Amerika Syarikat terus mengehadkan sentimen risiko. Pada 12:30 tengah hari, FBM KLCI susut 15.36 mata kepada 1,635.81 berbanding 1,651.17 pada penutupan Rabu. Indeks penanda aras itu dibuka 1.30 mata lebih rendah pada 1,649.87 sebelum bergerak antara 1,634.39 hingga 1,649.87 sepanjang sesi pagi. Kaunter Rugi Mendominasi Pasaran Sentimen keseluruhan kekal lemah apabila 583 kaunter mencatat penurunan berbanding 305 kaunter yang meningkat. Sebanyak 464 kaunter tidak berubah, manakala 1,421 kaunter tidak didagangkan dan 12 kaunter digantung. Jumlah dagangan mencapai 1.65 bilion saham bernilai RM1.18 bilion. Saham Bank Dan Tenaga Terus Tertekan Dalam kalangan saham berwajaran tinggi, Maybank dan Tenaga Nasional masing-masing susut 6 sen kepada RM9.93 dan RM12.90. Public Bank pula turun 4 sen kepada RM4.66, manakala CIMB berkurang 5 sen kepada RM7.74. IHH Healthcare turut susut 19 sen kepada RM7.64. Tekanan daripada kaunter berkapitalisasi besar ini menjadi antara faktor yang mengekang FBM KLCI pada sesi tengah hari. Data Pekerjaan AS Jadi Perhatian Apex Securities berkata sentimen pasaran turut terjejas selepas pengambilan pekerja sektor swasta AS meningkat lebih daripada jangkaan, dengan 90,000 pekerjaan ditambah pada September. Perkembangan tersebut mengimbangi kelegaan daripada data inflasi teras Personal Consumption Expenditures yang lebih rendah. Pelabur kini menunggu laporan Non-Farm Payrolls (NFP) AS pada Jumaat bagi mendapatkan petunjuk baharu mengenai hala tuju dasar Rizab Persekutuan AS. Pada masa sama, perkembangan rundingan Amerika Syarikat dan Iran serta pergerakan harga minyak turut menjadi perhatian pasaran. Zetrix AI Antara Kaunter Aktif Dalam dagangan aktif, Zetrix AI dan V.S Industry masing-masing meningkat setengah sen kepada 16.5 sen dan 28.5 sen. Jaks Resources pula susut setengah sen kepada 20 sen, manakala saham baharu ACE Market, GB Bond, turun 2.5 sen kepada 22.5 sen. Dagang Nexchange pula kembali mengukuh 1.5 sen kepada 50 sen. MPI Catat Kenaikan Terbesar Bagi kaunter untung, Malaysian Pacific Industries (MPI) menjadi antara yang mencatat kenaikan terbesar dengan menambah RM1.26 kepada RM41.66. MI Technovation pula meningkat 13 sen kepada RM5.33, diikuti Ta Ann yang naik 12 sen kepada RM5.92. Malayan Cement dan Genting Plantations masing-masing meningkat 11 sen dan 10 sen kepada RM5.56 dan RM5.63. KLK Antara Kaunter Paling Susut Sementara itu, Kuala Lumpur Kepong (KLK) mengetuai senarai kaunter rugi dengan susut 76 sen kepada RM21.44. Allianz Malaysia pula turun 62 sen kepada RM21, manakala Fraser & Neave, Hong Leong Industries dan Batu Kawan masing-masing berkurang 42 sen kepada RM21.32, RM16.04 dan RM20.10. Kebanyakan Indeks Dalam Zon Merah Di papan indeks, FBM Mid 70 susut 87.65 mata kepada 17,487.02, manakala FBM Emas turun 94.18 mata kepada 12,197.83. title: 'Bursa Malaysia Extends Losses at Midday On Selling Pressure
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 1 – Bursa Malaysia continued its downward trend at midday on Thursday, October 1, 2026, as selling pressure persisted across the board, tracking mixed global market performance amid rising United States Treasury yields. At 12:30 PM, the benchmark FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) slid 15.36 points to 1,635.81 compared to Wednesday’s close of 1,651.17. The main index opened 1.30 points lower at 1,649.87 and fluctuated between an intraday low of 1,634.39 and a high of 1,649.87 throughout the morning session. Broader market sentiment remained negative, with decliners outpacing gainers 583 to 305, while 464 counters traded unchanged, 1,421 untraded, and 12 suspended. Half-day turnover stood at 1.65 billion shares valued at RM1.18 billion. Heavyweights and Active Stocks Major banking, utility, and healthcare blue chips pulled the benchmark index lower: - IHH Healthcare contracted 19 sen to RM7.64. - Maybank and Tenaga Nasional lost 6 sen each to RM9.93 and RM12.90, respectively. - CIMB decreased 5 sen to RM7.74. - Public Bank fell 4 sen to RM4.66. Among active counters, Zetrix AI and V.S Industry both added half a sen to 16.5 sen and 28.5 sen, respectively. Dagang Nexchange rose 1.5 sen to 50 sen, while Jaks Resources eased half a sen to 20 sen and ACE Market debutant GB Bond dropped 2.5 sen to 22.5 sen. Technology and plantation counters featured among the top gainers: - Malaysian Pacific Industries: Advanced RM1.26 to RM41.66. - MI Technovation: Rose 13 sen to RM5.33. - Ta Ann: Accumulated 12 sen to RM5.92. - Malayan Cement: Strengthened 11 sen to RM5.56. - Genting Plantations: Improved 10 sen to RM5.63. Declining counters were led by Kuala Lumpur Kepong, which dropped 76 sen to RM21.44. Other notable pullbacks included Allianz Malaysia (down 62 sen to RM21.00), as well as Fraser & Neave, Hong Leong Industries, and Batu Kawan, which trimmed 42 sen each to RM21.32, RM16.04, and RM20.10, respectively. Index and Sectoral Performance All major sector indices posted declines at the midday break, led by financial services and plantation stocks: - The Financial Services Index dropped 148.77 points to 19,067.72. - The Plantation Index tumbled 121.85 points to 9,074.82. - The Energy Index eased 7.79 points to 837.91. - The Industrial Products and Services Index slipped 1.16 points to 178.80. Across broader market indices: - The FBM Top 100 Index fell 99.00 points to 11,985.44. - The FBM Emas Index declined 94.18 points to 12,197.83. - The FBM Emas Shariah Index weakened 87.69 points to 12,088.65. - The FBM Mid 70 Index dropped 87.65 points to 17,487.02. - The FBM ACE Index contracted 31.14 points to 5,503.14. –NMT

title: 'Malaysia’s freedom of information test
body: 'Malaysia’s proposed Freedom of Information Bill is under renewed scrutiny after civil society groups raised concerns over broad exemptions, existing secrecy laws and the effectiveness of its appeals process. A parliamentary town hall has now given stakeholders another opportunity to shape the legislation before it returns to Parliament. What needs to change for the bill to deliver genuine access to information, and can Malaysia balance greater government transparency with legitimate safeguards? title: 'Bursa dibuka rendah pada pagi ini
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR,. Bursa Malaysia dibuka rendah pada Khamis, menjejaki prestasi bercampur-campur Wall Street berikutan hasil bon Perbendaharaan AS yang lebih tinggi serta ketegangan berterusan di Asia Barat menjejaskan minat belian. Pada 9.10 pagi, FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) susut 3.74 mata atau 0.22 peratus kepada 1,647.43 daripada paras 1,651.17 ketika ditutup pada Rabu. Indeks penanda aras itu dibuka 1.30 mata lebih rendah pada 1,649.87. Di pasaran meluas, kaunter rugi mengatasi kaunter untung sebanyak 200 berbanding 142, manakala 307 kaunter tidak berubah, 2,124 kaunter tidak diniagakan dan 12 kaunter digantung. Jumlah dagangan sebanyak 246.59 juta saham bernilai RM118.14 juta. Naib Presiden Penyelidikan Ekuiti Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd, Thong Pak Leng, berkata Wall Street ditutup bercampur-campur apabila inflasi yang lebih rendah mengurangkan jangkaan terhadap satu lagi kenaikan kadar faedah oleh Rizab Persekutuan AS, meskipun hasil bon yang kekal tinggi terus menjejaskan sentimen. Di peringkat domestik, beliau berkata, indeks penanda aras pasaran mungkin cenderung diniagakan berhati-hati, dengan sentimen keseluruhan pasaran yang lemah dan jualan asing baru-baru ini menunjukkan pelabur terus mengambil pendekatan berhati-hati. “Justeru, bagi hari ini, kami menjangkakan indeks kekal dalam mod pengukuhan dalam julat 1,640-1,660, dengan aktiviti pembelian ketika harga rendah dijangka mengehadkan penurunan,” katanya kepada Bernama. Dalam kalangan saham wajaran tinggi, Maybank dan IHH Healthcare masing-masing tidak berubah pada RM9.90 dan RM7.83. Public Bank susut tiga sen kepada RM4.67, CIMB berkurangan satu sen kepada RM7.78 dan Tenaga Nasional turun dua sen kepada RM12.94. Dalam dagangan aktif, saham yang baru disenaraikan di Pasaran ACE, GB Bond susut setengah sen kepada 24.5 sen, manakala VS Industry tidak berubah pada 28 sen. Astro Malaysia menambah setengah sen kepada enam sen, Jaks Resources meningkat satu sen kepada 21.5 sen dan Divfex menokok dua sen kepada 11 sen. Antara kaunter untung utama, Keck Seng meningkat 11 sen kepada RM5.14 dan Petron Malaysia menambah tujuh sen kepada RM3.47. Hengyuan Refining dan Spritzer masing-masing naik enam sen kepada RM3.62 dan RM3.67, manakala Jati Tinggi mengukuh lima sen kepada RM1.44. Kuala Lumpur Kepong mendahului kaunter rugi apabila susut 18 sen kepada RM22.02. UWC pula berkurangan 15 sen kepada RM6.92, manakala Insights Analytics dan MISC masing-masing turun sembilan sen kepada RM1.20 dan RM7.55. Petronas Dagangan susut lapan sen kepada RM19.20. Di papan indeks, Indeks FBM Mid 70 susut 42.26 mata kepada 17,532.41, Indeks FBM Emas berkurangan 26.32 mata kepada 12,265.69, manakala Indeks FBM Top 100 turun 27.82 mata kepada 12,056.62. Indeks FBM Emas Shariah susut 22.09 mata kepada 12,154.26, manakala Indeks FBM ACE berkurangan 6.31 mata kepada 5,527.97. Mengikut sektor, Indeks Produk dan Perkhidmatan Perindustrian susut 0.10 mata kepada 180.31, manakala Indeks Tenaga meningkat 1.41 mata kepada 847.11. Indeks Perkhidmatan Kewangan turun 27.47 mata kepada 19,189.02, manakala Indeks Perladangan merosot 33.34 mata kepada 9,163.33. — BERNAMA

title: 'DNB lengkapkan pembiayaan RM5.2 bilion bagi menyokong fasa seterusnya pertumbuhan 5G | DagangNews - Berita Bisnes Anda
body: 'KUALA LUMPUR 1 Okt - Digital Nasional Bhd (DNB) melengkapkan pembiayaan berjangka Islam secara sindiket bernilai RM5.2 bilion, sekali gus mengukuhkan kedudukan pembiayaan jangka panjang syarikat ketika Malaysia memasuki fasa pertumbuhan seterusnya dwirangkaian 5G . DNB dalam kenyataan berkata pembiayaan itu akan memudahkan perancangan keluar Menteri Kewangan Diperbadankan (MOF Inc) sebagai pemegang saham biasa dan peralihan kepada pemilikan sama rata dalam kalangan pemegang saham pengendali rangkaian mudah alihnya, iaitu CelcomDigi Bhd, Maxis Broadband Sdn Bhd dan YTL Power International Bhd. Peralihan pemilikan tersebut dijangka berlaku pada awal suku keempat 2026, manakala MOF Inc akan mengekalkan saham khas dalam DNB bagi melindungi kepentingan negara. Pembiayaan berkenaan turut merangkumi pembiayaan semula kemudahan kredit pusingan DNB yang dijamin kerajaan dan tamat tempoh pada 29 September, selain mewujudkan struktur pembiayaan jangka panjang bagi menyokong pertumbuhan syarikat. Penyempurnaan pembiayaan itu bertepatan dengan pemberian penuh spektrum 100MHz dalam jalur 3.3–3.4GHz serta penukaran keseluruhan pegangan spektrum 240MHz DNB kepada penetapan spektrum. Penetapan oleh Suruhanjaya Komunikasi dan Multimedia Malaysia (MCMC) itu berkuat kuasa mulai 1 Oktober. Menurut DNB, blok spektrum 240MHz tersebut akan meningkatkan kapasiti, kecekapan dan prestasi rangkaian, selain menyokong teknologi termasuk Massive MIMO, pengagregatan pembawa, 5G Advanced dan keupayaan rangkaian dipacu kecerdasan buatan. Ketua Pegawai Eksekutif DNB, Datuk Azman Ismail berkata pembiayaan berkenaan menyediakan platform mampan untuk syarikat beroperasi secara bebas sambil meneruskan pelaburan dalam peningkatan rangkaian dan peluasan kapasiti. “Penyempurnaan pembiayaan RM5.2 bilion ini merupakan pencapaian penting bagi DNB dan mencerminkan keyakinan kukuh terhadap asas perniagaan, rekod operasi serta peranan jangka panjang kami dalam ekonomi digital Malaysia,” katanya. Maybank Investment Bank Bhd bertindak sebagai pengatur utama yang diberi mandat, pengurus buku dan pengatur penyelaras bagi pembiayaan itu. AmInvestment Bank Bhd, CIMB Islamic Bank Bhd, RHB Islamic Bank Bhd dan United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd pula merupakan pengatur utama bersama yang diberi mandat, manakala AmInvestment Bank bertindak sebagai penasihat kewangan DNB. - DagangNews.com
